result:
There is a brief, miraculous window just before dawn when the world belongs to no one. The streetlights buzz with a tired hum, amber islands against the indigo dark, while the houses remain blind, their curtained windows holding the slow, rhythmic breathing of sleepers. Outside, the air smells of chilled earth, wet asphalt, and the sharp, invisible promise of morning.

In this suspended hour, time forgets its urgency. You can stand on a porch with steam rising from a mug and feel entirely untethered from history, obligations, and the frantic machinery of noon. A solitary bird—usually a robin or a sparrow whose internal clock runs slightly fast—tests the silence with a tentative, crystalline note. It does not cascade into a full chorus; it simply asks if anyone else is awake. When no answer comes, it settles back into the leaves, content to wait.

Soon enough, the blue will pale to gray, and gray will bruise into peach and gold along the horizon. Engines will turn over, sirens will remind the streets of human fragility, and the collective noise of survival will resume. But for ten or fifteen minutes, existence is pure potential. Yesterday’s failures have dissolved into the dark, and today’s demands have not yet crossed the threshold. To be awake in this quiet is to witness the universe taking a long, deep breath before the curtain rises, offering a rare gift: the fleeting chance to exist entirely unnoticed, quietly suspended between what was and all that might yet be.
